items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: Judah Smith Is More Interested in Reaching the World Than Building a Bigger Church
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Years ago, Judah Smith was reading Luke 7 when a detail stopped him. Jesus is eating at the home of Simon the Pharisee when a woman comes in, pours perfume on His feet and wipes them with her hair. Simon is scandalized. Jesus answers him, but Luke makes a point of saying Jesus is looking…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Years ago, Judah Smith was reading Luke 7 when a detail stopped him.

Jesus is eating at the home of Simon the Pharisee when a woman comes in, pours perfume on His feet and wipes them with her hair. Simon is scandalized. Jesus answers him, but Luke makes a point of saying Jesus is looking at the woman.

“God, why are you talking to Simon but looking at the woman?” Smith remembers asking.

“God said, ‘This is what I’ve asked of you. I’m gonna ask you to face the world. You’ll still speak to the Church, but I want you to face the world.’”

For years, the Churchome pastor has occupied an unusual place in American Christianity. He preaches to packed rooms and built a massive digital audience, and he’s also known for his friendships with some of the most famous people in entertainment and sports. Justin Bieber has spoken openly about Smith’s influence on his faith. Lana Del Rey recorded part of a Smith sermon at church and put it on an album. Behind the scenes, the list goes on.

Those relationships have made him an easy target. “Celebrity pastor” is rarely meant as a compliment.

Smith knows the criticism, and he thinks it misses what he’s actually trying to do.

“I’ve always felt called to Rome,” he says, using the empire as shorthand for the wider culture. “I’ve always felt like I wanted to win with Rome. I always felt like Rome are my people.”

He still obviously considers himself part of the Church. He’s just stopped measuring his ministry by how many people it can get into one room on a Sunday.

“I’m not really hung up on, I wanna fill a bunch of churches,” he says. “I want people to be in community, but man, we gotta get the message out. We’ve got the greatest story to tell.”

He has spent the last several years experimenting with what that looks like. Churchome went hard into digital ministry and put millions into an app. Smith has hosted gatherings outside traditional church settings, and he’s now working on a sprawling first-person retelling of the biblical story.

“What if we took all the traditions off and what if we took a lot of the rules off?” he says. “What if it wasn’t moralism and elitism? And what if it wasn’t colluded with the policymakers of particular countries or continents? And what if it was just, let’s just give them Jesus?”

It’s also why he doesn’t apologize for spending time with people who have enormous platforms. Some of his famous friends tease him for how little he posts about them.

“Protection is primary,” he says.

Sometimes that’s a text. Sometimes it’s listening to someone unload something painful and never repeating it to anyone. Mostly it’s being a safe presence for someone whose life has very few private corners left.

“If the platform grows, the pain grows,” he says. “It is a parallel every single time.”

He’s watched people get the thing everyone assumes will make life easier, and then discover the bigger the audience, the harder it is to find anyone they can trust when the cameras are off.

It changed the way he pastors, too.

For years, he says, he took the expectation of being “the leader” too seriously. Relationships ran one direction. He was the one with the answers, the one doing the encouraging, the one who was fine.

“At some point, I need to connect with them too as a follower, and I need to open my heart,” he says.

Now he tries to let relationships move both ways, including with people he once saw only as people he was supposed to lead. That means admitting when he’s struggling instead of keeping up the idea that pastors have somehow graduated from ordinary human emotion.

“It’s impossible for me to be OK every day,” Smith says. “That’s not even real. There’s no chance that’s real. I get the sense sometimes us preachers, we feel like we gotta be OK every day. No, we don’t. Says who?”

That shift has a starting point. In October 2007, he says, a phrase came to him while he was wrestling with how he understood ministry: “Grace grows the church.”

“And everything changed for me,” he says. “It started to just unwind.”

What unwound was the performance-driven version of Christianity that Smith now believes his generation of pastors helped reinforce without meaning to.

“We live in a do-good, get-good scenario,” he says. “I don’t think anyone ever intended to dilute the glorious message of Jesus, but we did.”

Churches got good at practical preaching, he argues. People learned how to improve their marriages, manage their lives and become better versions of themselves. None of it was bad. But Smith worries about what people heard underneath it.

“I need to try a little harder. I need to pray more. I need to give more. I need to serve more.”

“God is not the football coach,” he says.

Smith’s book Bad Thoughts, written with psychologist Les Parrott and published last fall, grew partly out of his own effort to untangle those patterns. He and his wife, Chelsea, began meeting with Parrott, and Smith eventually joked that they should write a book about “all the things you fixed in me.”

The book lands roughly where his thinking about ministry has: “Stop earning credit with God and just receive His gift.”

Smith still wants people in churches. He still preaches, and he still pastors. He’s just not interested in building a ministry that ends at the church door.

“I want people to know His story,” he says.

These days, he’s mostly trying to make sure he’s facing the right direction when he tells it.

items.title: On Not Seeing It All: Bishop Barron’s ‘Heaven in Stone and Glass’
items.author: Dr. Tod Worner
items.summary:
Dr. Tod Worner

It is what the cathedral offers that exceeds what the cathedral is. Bishop Barron's film brings this back in sharp relief.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tod Worner

“I just can’t see it all!”

People nearby looked at me strangely. Why wouldn’t they? Arching my back in an impossibly contortionist style and staring vertiginously into the heavens, my words spilled out in groans. But try as I might, from the structure’s vast footings, I just couldn’t quite capture the entirety of this majestic cathedral. Cologne Cathedral was simply too tall. Straightening up and looking around, I saw a long-haired street artist masterfully chalking a portrait of the Virgin Mary on the stone parvis. Tourists sporting their windbreakers and fanny packs milled about snapping pictures. And an oversized photo board boasted a World War II–era aerial shot with the cathedral’s defiant spires jousting the air while everything around them was reduced to ashen wreckage. 

There was no mistaking it: Everyone was here for the cathedral.

I don’t know when I first fell in love with architecture, but it must have been that visit. Traveling throughout Europe on a college choir tour, we sang in some of the most soaring and sublime venues: Cologne Cathedral, Notre Dame, Chartres, and the Basilica of the Sacred Heart of Montmartre, among others. It was otherworldly. Singing in Cologne Cathedral, an architectural wonder that took 632 years to build. Harmonizing in Notre Dame, where the music of liturgical masters reverberated off its limestone walls for centuries. Vocalizing in Chartres, bathed softly in the light of the rose windows.

With their enormous pillars and mathematically precise arches, flying buttresses and tiled labyrinths, soaring spires and bellowing bell towers, ornate facades and brilliant windows, these cathedrals are more than sublime—they are a reminder of our Christian story: The Lord became incarnate; the Lord died on a cross; the Lord rose from the dead . . . for you. And as the bells would toll, they cried, “Come to Mass. Partake in the sacraments. Worship your Lord. Ease your mind. Be free. Be free.”  

In those moments, I became Catholic. And I didn’t even know it. 

Bishop Robert Barron’s incomparable Heaven in Stone and Glass brings all of this back in sharp relief. This film is a tale of formation. But not the formation you expect. To be sure, the consuming fire at Notre Dame Cathedral and its rebuilding figure centrally. The designs of Chartres, Notre Dame, Reims, Amiens, and Saint-Denis are also unfolded. But lest one get caught up in the story of architecture—the very formation of stone and glass and marble—one might miss the greater story: the formation of the soul. For this film is about how you and I are formed by the beautiful. Namely, it is a film about how we are formed by timeless cathedrals and their ornate artistry that tells the story, offers the Mass, and houses the parishioners against the buffeting winds of fear and worry, war and revolution, pain and sickness, and the darkness of death. 

It is one thing to say that the cathedrals are beautiful, for they are. Ask your favorite architect to tour with you, and you will marvel at the mathematical achievements. Invite your trusted museum docent to unpack the paintings and windows, sculptures and statuary, and you will wonder with an artist’s appreciation. A cathedral is more than beautiful. It is holy. Enlivened by the Eucharist, edified by the sacraments, breathing with the Body of Christ, and pregnant with missionary zeal, it is what the cathedral offers that exceeds what the cathedral is. 

It is not simply stone and glass. 

It is heaven in stone and glass.

In his timeless work, Orthodoxy, G. K. Chesterton captured this point brilliantly:

Christ prophesied the whole of Gothic architecture in that hour when nervous and respectable people. . . objected to the shouting of the gutter-snipes of Jerusalem. He said, “If these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” Under the impulse of His spirit arose like a clamorous chorus the facades of the mediaeval cathedrals, thronged with shouting faces and open mouths. The prophecy has fulfilled itself: the very stones cry out.

Next year, I will return to Europe over three decades after my first visit. And when I do, thanks to Bishop Barron’s exquisite film, I will see the cathedrals once again, but I will also see them anew. Once again, I’ll stand at the footings, arch my back (embarrassing my daughters), and groan, “I just can’t see it all!”

With heaven in this stone and glass, will we ever?
